nameStory: The word 'lilac' comes from the Persian word 'nilak,' meaning bluish, which traveled through Arabic and French before reaching English. This fragrant shrub earned its 'common' designation because it became so widely planted that it seemed to grow everywhere, even though it's actually native to the Balkan Peninsula in southeastern Europe.
description: Common lilac is a beloved deciduous shrub that can grow 8-15 feet tall and wide, forming dense clumps over time. It's famous for its incredibly fragrant, cone-shaped flower clusters that bloom in late spring, typically in shades of purple, pink, or white. The heart-shaped leaves are smooth and arranged in opposite pairs along sturdy branches. You'll often find old lilac bushes still thriving around abandoned farmhouses and cellar holes throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, pyramid-shaped clusters of tiny four-petaled flowers with an unmistakably sweet, intoxicating fragrance that can be smelled from yards away. Each small flower has a tube-like base that opens into four flat petals.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves, 2-5 inches long, with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel. They're arranged in opposite pairs and remain bright green through summer with no fall color to speak of.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, multi-stemmed clumps that spread by suckers, creating thickets over time. Branches are sturdy and grayish-brown with a slightly rough texture.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry brown capsules that split open to release winged seeds. These persist through winter and rattle when shaken, clustered where the flowers used to be.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, plump buds that are greenish-brown and feel firm to the touch. They're arranged opposite each other and are quite noticeable in winter.

habitat: Common lilac thrives in well-drained, slightly alkaline soils and loves full sun. In New England, you'll most often find it around old homesites, farmsteads, and cemeteries where it was planted generations ago and continues to spread. It's quite hardy and can tolerate poor soils, which is why it persists so well in abandoned areas.

seasonality.spring: The spectacular flower show happens in May, with intensely fragrant blooms that last about 2-3 weeks. This is prime identification time when the sweet perfume fills the air.
seasonality.summer: Green heart-shaped leaves provide identification, while spent flowers develop into small seed capsules. The shrub looks fairly ordinary during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves remain green late into fall before dropping with little color change. The brown seed capsules become more noticeable as they dry and split open.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the multi-stemmed growth habit and prominent opposite buds. Dried seed clusters often persist, rattling in the wind.

funFact: Lilac flowers with five petals instead of the usual four are considered extremely lucky to find - tradition says you should eat the five-petaled flower and make a wish, though finding one among thousands of four-petaled blooms is genuinely rare!
confusionNotes: Young lilacs might be confused with other heart-leaved shrubs, but nothing else has that distinctive sweet fragrance combined with opposite heart-shaped leaves. Remember: if it doesn't smell heavenly in bloom, it's not a lilac!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' and seeming native to New England, lilacs are actually European imports that have naturalized so successfully they feel like part of the landscape. Many of the massive lilac bushes you see are likely over 100 years old, planted by settlers who brought them for their beauty and fragrance.
compareHints: Common lilac blooms earlier than Japanese tree lilac and has the classic sweet fragrance, while tree lilac has a honey-like scent and blooms in June. Hungarian lilac has narrower leaves and a more upright growth habit, and Korean lilac stays much smaller and more compact. The heart-shaped leaves and incredible fragrance are your best clues for identifying common lilac.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Japanese tree lilac is easily distinguished from common lilac and other shrubby lilacs by its tree form and creamy-white, honey-scented flowers that bloom much later in the season.
Hungarian lilac differs from common lilac in its much thicker, leathery leaves, later bloom time, and more upright growth habit.
Korean lilac is much more compact than common lilac, staying under 6 feet versus 15+ feet, and has smaller, fuzzier leaves.
